A.why: The list of achievements made you expect one of them next. The finger exercises are not among the listed achievements, and the sentence ranks them above everything listed.

B.why: You assumed that a long list of successes leads to a conclusion. Her violins and treatise do not explain why she valued the exercises most, so 'Thus' invents a cause.

C.why: This is the list trap. 'Indeed' intensifies the previous point, as if the next sentence named an even grander success. The sentence instead calls her favourite achievement 'modest' and ranks it above the impressive list, so it turns against the list.

items.subtype_name: Expectation, then surprise (However / Nonetheless / That said / Actually)
items.stimulus: Seismologists once assumed that, during any earthquake, the buildings nearest the epicenter would always shake hardest. ______ in 1985, an earthquake centered roughly 350 kilometers from Mexico City toppled hundreds of buildings there while towns far closer to the epicenter suffered less, because the city rests on soft lakebed sediments that amplified the seismic waves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence states an old assumption. The second gives a real event that disproves it: distant buildings fell while nearer towns did better. When a mistaken belief is followed by what actually happened, 'In reality' is the correction word.

B.why: You saw a single dated event and treated it as an illustration. An example has to support the claim before it, and this event is a counterexample that disproves the assumption.

C.why: You noticed the 'because' and the cause-and-effect language about sediments and carried it back to the blank. The seismologists' assumption did not lead to the 1985 damage. The damage contradicts the assumption.

D.why: Both sentences are about how hard buildings shake, so you read them as moving in the same direction. 'Likewise' would need the second sentence to support the assumption, but it overturns it.
